item.title: Do Similarities or Differences Foster Marital Happiness?
item.description:
Marriage

Do Similarities or Differences Foster Marital Happiness?

Whether similarity fosters marital satisfaction gets more complicated over time.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • When it comes to choosing a partner, research finds that opposites don't attract.
  • The Similarity-Attraction Hypothesis holds for couples from physical attraction to education.
  • Aging changes the needs and the necessary skills of partners such that similarities are not enough.
  • To function better as a couple over time, different complimentary skills and assets matter.

The question of whether similar or dissimilar personality traits are a source of romantic attraction and marital satisfaction has been debated for years.

An extensive study by Horowitz et al. in Nature Human Behavior (2023) reports significant correlations between human partners based on systematic reviews and meta-analyses of 22 traits and UK Biobank analysis of 133 traits. Essentially, it finds that people connect based on similarity. Opposites don’t attract.

Consistent with this, the Similarity-Attraction Hypothesis seems to hold up across characteristics such as physical attractiveness, attachment style, political and religious attitudes, and level of education. It even holds up in terms of the attraction of thrill-seeking or sensation-seeking people to each other.

One thrill-seeking couple had their first date at an Amusement Park, where they rode a 325-foot roller coaster 12 times. They agreed when making wedding plans that the Fury 325 was the perfect place to say, “ I do,” so they did just that. Who knows how the wedding party coped!

Similarity-Attraction Hypothesis Over Time

While the initial benefit of Similarity-Attraction is clear, it does not seem to hold up over time.

A 2007 study reported in Psychology and Aging entitled “Birds of a Feather Don’t Always Fly Farthest” sheds some light on this (Shiota and Levenson, 2007).

Shiota and Levenson (2007) conducted one of the first studies to explicitly consider age as a potential moderator of the link between similarity and satisfaction. The authors were able to evaluate the “birds of a feather flock together” hypothesis, both for initial levels of relationship satisfaction and for predictions of marital satisfaction trajectories over time, for both middle-aged and older couples.

They examined similarity in the Big Five Personality Factors in couples across the years. These included:

  • Openness to Experience vs. Close-minded
  • Conscientious vs. Disorganized
  • Extroverted vs. Introverted
  • Agreeable vs. Disagreeable
  • Nervous vs. Calm and Relaxed

The surprising finding is that, whereas similarity of personality traits resulted in more marital satisfaction in the early years, couples with similar traits reported less satisfaction in the middle and later years.

Reconsider and Use the Differences

Couples might consider that although they both have similarities, life brings with it physical, emotional, and lifestyle challenges that demand different skills, reactions, and experience. Calling upon their diverse skills and/or perspectives that were not needed or not apparent in the early years can give them an advantage in the later years, as they become a “complementary couple.”

Yes, they both love to travel, but one is far better than the other at setting up the trip; or one is calmer with the youngest grandchildren, while the other actually likes being with the teens. Both are anxious with money and medical decisions, but recognizing different strengths offers the benefit of two perspectives unfolding into a third and better one.

They are the same birds of a feather, but they are flying together to unexpected places in very different ways. Generally, when people are faced with unknowns, they get anxious, and when people get anxious, their dysregulation unfolds as anger. An alternative is to get curious and benefit from the differences you find in your partner.

Hang on with love. There is always another roller coaster ride. It’s different, but you can find a way to hang on together.

item.title: Telling Your Donor-Conceived Child Their Story Early Matters
item.description:
Infertility

Telling Your Donor-Conceived Child Their Story Early Matters

Your donor-conceived child does not need to understand their story to hear it.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Waiting until your child can understand their story may not be the best strategy.
  • Talking to your child early and often can help them feel secure in who they are.
  • Sharing your child's story, as early as possible, can improve your bond with them.
  • Practicing the story when your child is young helps you get more comfortable talking about it.
Source: senivpetro/Freepik

After hearing from the experiences of adopted children and then later relearning very similar lessons from donor-conceived children, people are more commonly understanding that children do best when they learn their origin stories early. As a result, more people are talking to their children earlier.

I completely understand the hesitation. Being a parent of children who are not genetically connected to me, and having seen thousands of people using donor conception to build their families, I understand it is typically not a comfortable or familiar conversation to have.

Most of us did not grow up knowing people who used donor conception to build their families, so it is something that may feel different or “other.”

People who have had infertility typically feel the pain the most acutely, but even queer couples and single parents by choice may find it difficult to use the genetics of someone they don’t know to build one of the most intimate relationships of their lives, and then tell a story about it.

These stressors are often layered on top of the stressors commonly felt by fertility patients, such as the cost, the inconvenience, feeling out of control never knowing when (or if) it will work, managing your schedule around treatment and the stress of coping if it doesn’t go well, or takes longer than expected.

So when the baby comes, some of the pain may still be present, but for many, there is a natural desire to put the stressful moments away, finally enjoy parenthood and not revisit one more uncomfortable conversation. Yet, having those conversations early may save you, your partner, and your child from problems in the future.

Many people say they want to wait until their child can fully understand. Some single parents-to-be and queer couples tell me that they don’t need to tell their child early because it will be obvious to the child. Here are a few reasons why telling your child before they can fully understand their story can be so helpful.

Practice Helps You Make the Story Your Own

For the reasons just described, it makes sense that a parent might feel uncomfortable sharing their child’s story. In this state, a parent may feel awkward, trip over their words or even shed some tears. While that is perfectly understandable, the child does not understand their parents’ reaction. So, they will not think, “my parents love me so they are trying to get this right.” They are more likely to think, “when my parents raise this topic, they act so strange, I wonder if there is something wrong with it, or with me."

As with most things in life, practicing will help. Rehearsing with your partner or friends, trying books that you think you may like and giving yourself permission to have your tears, stumble, and rewrite your story allows you to mold it so it feels like yours. This can help you get the kinks out and make it more comfortable for you and for your child.

Telling the Story Early Helps Your Child to Feel Secure About Who They Are

We know that donor conceived children, like adopted children, don’t want a formal sit-down meeting. In fact, many say their wish is to never remember a day where they heard it for the first time. They want the words and the warm feelings behind the story to just be part of the backdrop of their life.

Donor-conceived and adopted children site two reasons for this. First, they want to feel connected to their parents, and if they feel something is withheld from them, they may wonder if there is something to be ashamed of, and they may also wonder if there are other things that are being kept from them. Second, some donor-conceived children have reported that they experience identity confusion. We know from people, like the actress Keri Washington and many others, that this is not universal, but it is possible for the child to grow up looking at their parents as their genetic connections, and when they discover someone else was involved in helping to create them, they may need to recalibrate their sense of who they are. Their sense of identity is affected, and they can feel a kind of crisis as a result.

We have seen that children who learn early and whose parents return to the story often and naturally over time, tend to feel more secure in themselves and closer to their parents.

Final Thoughts

It may seem like talking to your baby about their origins early is not important because your child is too young to understand, but what matters most is for you to get comfortable with the story so it eventually becomes an easy part of play or family conversations. These small investments will not only help your child feel more secure in who they are, and the way they were created, but are likely to do wonders for your relationship with them too.
